# America's Favorite Cities: The Verdict Is In

*(Travel + Leisure)* -- It comes as little surprise that Americans hold strong opinions—particularly when it comes to the cities they call home and the destinations they visit. These sentiments run so deep that in the 2008 America's Favorite Cities survey, conducted by travelandleisure.com and CNN Headline News, participants cast more than 600,000 votes across 45 characteristics spanning 25 cities. Categories ranged from shopping, dining, culture, and nightlife to cleanliness and affordability, with New Orleans claiming top honors for both fine dining and live music.

The 2007 results sparked considerable celebration among cities that secured top rankings—Chicago, Illinois, for its dining scene, and Austin, Texas, for its acclaimed singles scene. Yet the survey also produced its share of upsets, and, inevitably, its share of disappointment. The proud residents of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, found themselves ranked dead last in the "attractive people" category, while Los Angeles, California claimed the dubious distinction of least friendly city—a title many had expected New York City to earn.

## Notable Shifts

This year's rankings brought several surprises to the forefront. New Orleans, Louisiana, unseated New York as the premier destination for fine dining, while Las Vegas, Nevada, claimed the top spot for best singles scene, relegating former champion Austin to fifth place. In the cleanliness category, Portland, Oregon, displaced longtime leader Minneapolis, Minnesota, to claim the No. 1 position.

*See all the America's Favorite Cities results—and play the new AFC game, "What's YOUR Fave?"*

Other cities, however, held firm to their reigning titles. New York retained its crown as the nation's premier destination for people-watching, while Charleston, South Carolina, was once again crowned America's friendliest city.

## Finding Your Perfect Getaway

Beyond the rankings themselves, there's much more to discover. For travelers seeking their ideal destination, the Vacation Finder at travelandleisure.com offers personalized guidance based on individual interests. Austin and New Orleans, for instance, stand out as vibrant destinations offering live music, affordable ethnic cuisine, and vintage shopping.

For those with more refined sensibilities, Washington, D.C. (ranked No. 1 for museums) and New York (No. 1 for classical music) present compelling options. Travelers who crave both urban sophistication and outdoor adventure should consider Honolulu, Hawaii (No. 1 for active/adventure vacations), Portland (No. 1 for public parks and outdoor access), or Denver, Colorado (No. 1 for athletic, active residents).

Families traveling with children will find Orlando, Florida, remains the top choice, though San Diego, California, and Washington, D.C., continue to earn high marks as worthy alternatives. Those seeking romance, meanwhile, might try their luck in Honolulu, Charleston, or San Francisco, California—each offering its own distinct allure.

## What Became of the Bottom Rankings?

Did Philadelphia manage to rally public opinion and climb the attractiveness rankings? Did Angelenos take the criticism about civility to heart, adopting friendlier gestures on the freeway? Read on to discover the answers.

Continue below for the **top three cities** in select categories, as voted by visitors. For complete results—covering both the best and worst performers in every category, as ranked by both residents and visitors—visit travelandleisure.com.

## Cast Your Vote: "What's YOUR Fave?"

You've weighed in on individual city characteristics—but which city reigns supreme overall? Make your voice heard in our new bracket-style competition, "What's YOUR Fave?" Visit travelandleisure.com/afc, where over the next four weeks, we'll pit cities against one another head-to-head. Your votes will determine which cities advance and which are eliminated from contention!

# America's Favorite Cities 2008: A Shifting Landscape of Urban Rankings

The travel and lifestyle landscape of American cities underwent significant transformation in 2008, according to the results of the America's Favorite Cities survey conducted jointly by Travel + Leisure (travelandleisure.com) and CNN Headline News. This extensive survey compiled the opinions of everyday travelers and residents, gathering more than 600,000 votes across 45 distinct characteristics that ranged from culinary excellence to social atmosphere. Twenty-five major U.S. cities were evaluated in this comprehensive assessment, offering a fascinating snapshot of how American perceptions of urban destinations were evolving.

## Culinary Capital Shifts South

Perhaps the most notable upset in the 2008 rankings came from the world of fine dining. New Orleans, the vibrant Louisiana city renowned for its rich culinary heritage and jazz-infused culture, claimed the top spot for both fine dining and live music. In doing so, the city accomplished something remarkable: it dethroned New York City, long considered the unrivaled epicenter of American gastronomy, from its position as the nation's premier dining destination. This shift signaled a broader recognition of New Orleans' culinary resurgence and its unique blend of Creole, Cajun, and international influences that had captivated food enthusiasts nationwide.

## Unexpected Rankings Shake Up Perceptions

The survey results also delivered some surprising and, in certain cases, unflattering distinctions. Philadelphia found itself at the bottom of the rankings in the attractive people category, a designation that likely raised eyebrows among the City of Brotherly Love's residents and boosters. Meanwhile, in perhaps the most unexpected result of the entire survey, Los Angeles—a city synonymous with celebrity culture and Hollywood glamour—was voted the least friendly city in America. This ranking defied conventional wisdom, as many observers had anticipated New York City, with its reputation for brusque interactions and fast-paced lifestyle, would claim this less-than-desirable title instead.

## Nightlife and Cleanliness Change Hands

The competitive landscape for nightlife also saw considerable movement. Las Vegas, the entertainment capital known for its round-the-clock excitement and vibrant social scene, wrested the title of best singles scene away from Austin, Texas, which had previously held this distinction. This transition highlighted Las Vegas's growing appeal not just as a gambling destination but as a genuine hub for singles seeking connection and entertainment.

In matters of civic pride and urban maintenance, Portland, Oregon, emerged as the new standard-bearer for cleanliness, surpassing Minneapolis, which had previously held this honor. This shift underscored Portland's reputation for environmental consciousness and meticulous urban planning, qualities that resonated strongly with survey respondents.

## Consistency Amid Change

Despite these numerous shifts and surprises, certain cities managed to maintain their established reputations. New York City, notwithstanding its loss of the fine dining crown, continued to reign supreme as the best city for people-watching—a testament to its endlessly diverse population and bustling street life that offers endless opportunities for observation and fascination.

Similarly, Charleston, South Carolina, once again secured its position as America's friendliest city, reinforcing the Southern charm and hospitality for which this historic coastal city has long been celebrated. This repeat honor demonstrated that, amid all the changes and upsets throughout the rankings, Charleston's warm reputation remained a constant and reliable fixture in the American urban landscape.

## Conclusion

The 2008 America's Favorite Cities survey painted a picture of an American urban environment in flux, where traditional powerhouses like New York faced legitimate challenges to their supremacy, while other cities either solidified their standing or experienced unexpected reversals in public perception. These results offered valuable insights into changing American attitudes toward urban living, dining, socializing, and civic pride during this particular moment in the nation's cultural history.

# The American Approach to Travel and Leisure

Travel and leisure occupy a significant place in American culture, reflecting both the nation's diverse landscape and its evolving relationship with work-life balance. For many Americans, vacation time represents a cherished opportunity to explore new destinations, reconnect with family, and step away from the demands of daily routines.

## Domestic Adventures

The United States itself offers remarkable diversity for travelers, from the beaches of Florida and California to the mountains of Colorado and the national parks scattered across the country. Road trips remain a quintessential American tradition, embodying a sense of freedom and adventure that dates back to the early days of automobile travel. National parks like Yellowstone, Yosemite, and the Grand Canyon draw millions of visitors annually, allowing Americans to experience natural wonders within their own borders.

## International Exploration

Beyond domestic travel, many Americans also seek international experiences, whether visiting popular destinations in Europe, exploring the Caribbean, or venturing to more distant locations in Asia and beyond. International travel has grown increasingly accessible, though Americans generally take fewer vacation days compared to their counterparts in many other developed nations, a reflection of workplace culture that often prioritizes productivity over extended time off.

## Changing Leisure Patterns

Leisure activities among Americans have evolved significantly over recent decades. While traditional pursuits like camping, visiting theme parks, and beach vacations remain popular, there's been growing interest in experiential travel—seeking authentic cultural immersion, culinary adventures, and outdoor recreation like hiking and adventure sports. Wellness tourism has also gained traction, with many seeking retreats focused on relaxation and rejuvenation.

## Economic and Social Dimensions

Travel and leisure represent substantial economic activity in the United States, supporting industries ranging from hospitality and transportation to entertainment. However, access to travel opportunities isn't uniform across the population; income levels, job flexibility, and geographic location all influence how and whether Americans can pursue leisure travel.

## Conclusion

Ultimately, travel and leisure remain deeply woven into American life, serving as both a reflection of cultural values and a means of personal enrichment. Whether through weekend getaways, family road trips, or international adventures, these experiences continue to shape how Americans relate to their country and the wider world, even as patterns of travel continue to shift with changing economic conditions and societal priorities.

# Travel & Leisure Survey Ranks America's Best (and Worst) Cities Across Key Categories

A comprehensive survey conducted by Travel and Leisure magazine, in partnership with CNN, has ranked American cities across a range of categories including dining, nightlife, friendliness, and overall attractiveness, offering travelers a fresh look at how the nation's top destinations stack up against one another.

The survey, which polled thousands of travelers on their experiences and perceptions of major U.S. cities, sought to move beyond simple popularity contests and instead measure specific qualities that make a city appealing—or unappealing—to visitors.

## Dining and Nightlife Take Center Stage

Unsurprisingly, cities long celebrated for their culinary scenes and after-dark entertainment options performed well in those respective categories. Cities known for diverse restaurant offerings, innovative chefs, and vibrant food cultures scored highly in the dining category, while those with reputations for lively bars, clubs, and live music venues topped the nightlife rankings.

Travelers noted that a city's dining reputation often correlated with its overall desirability as a destination, suggesting that food tourism continues to play an increasingly important role in how Americans choose where to spend their vacation time and money.

## Friendliness Factor

Perhaps one of the more subjective categories, "friendliness," asked respondents to rate how welcoming and approachable locals were during their visits. Southern cities and smaller metropolitan areas tended to perform well in this category, with survey respondents citing warm hospitality and a relaxed pace of life as contributing factors.

Larger, busier metropolitan hubs, by contrast, sometimes scored lower in friendliness, even when they excelled in other categories like dining or cultural attractions—highlighting a common trade-off travelers identified between big-city excitement and small-town warmth.

## Attractiveness and Aesthetic Appeal

The attractiveness category evaluated cities based on their physical beauty, architecture, natural surroundings, and overall visual appeal. Coastal cities and those with distinctive skylines or historic architecture generally fared well, as did cities that have invested heavily in public parks, waterfronts, and urban beautification projects in recent years.

## What the Rankings Mean for Travelers

The Travel and Leisure/CNN survey serves as a useful tool for travelers weighing options for future trips, particularly those looking to prioritize specific experiences—whether that's a food-focused getaway, a nightlife-heavy weekend, or a relaxing visit to a picturesque, welcoming destination.

Industry analysts note that such rankings can also influence local tourism boards and city planners, who often use survey results to identify areas for improvement or to bolster marketing campaigns highlighting a city's strengths.

While rankings and surveys are inherently subjective and shaped by the preferences of those polled, the Travel and Leisure/CNN results offer a snapshot of how everyday travelers perceive America's urban destinations—and provide plenty of food for thought for anyone planning their next getaway.

*Results and detailed city-by-city breakdowns can be found on travelandleisure.com.*

# America's Favorite Cities: The Results Are In (And the Debate Is Just Getting Started)

There's nothing quite like a good hometown rivalry to get people fired up, and America's Favorite Cities survey has once again proven that when it comes to urban pride, the competition is fierce. From the jazz-soaked streets of the French Quarter to the neon glow of the Strip, this year's rankings have sparked plenty of conversation—and more than a few friendly arguments.

## The Big Easy Charms Again

**New Orleans** continues to hold a special place in America's heart, and it's not hard to see why. The city's unmatched blend of live music pouring out of every corner bar, food that ranges from beignets to gumbo to po'boys, and a cultural richness you simply can't manufacture keeps it near the top of favorite-city lists year after year. Whether it's Mardi Gras madness or a quiet Sunday brunch with a side of brass band, New Orleans delivers an experience that feels genuinely one-of-a-kind.

## Vegas Baby, Vegas

Then there's **Las Vegas**, the city that never apologizes for being over the top. Sin City continues to dazzle survey respondents with its "anything goes" energy—world-class shows, celebrity chef restaurants, and a nightlife scene that literally never sleeps. Love it or find it exhausting, Vegas remains a magnetic force that pulls in visitors chasing that particular brand of desert-fueled excitement.

## Philly's Underdog Appeal

**Philadelphia** often gets overshadowed by flashier East Coast neighbors, but this year's survey suggests that's changing. Cheesesteak debates aside, Philly's deep historical roots, thriving art scene, and passionate (if occasionally rowdy) sports culture are winning over respondents who appreciate a city with substance and grit. It's the kind of place that rewards you for digging a little deeper.

## L.A.'s Enduring Allure

Whether you're chasing beach views in Santa Monica or tacos in Boyle Heights, L.A.'s sprawling diversity keeps landing it high on America's list of beloved destinations.

# America's Cities, Ranked: Where to Find Love, Cleanliness, and a Good People-Watching Bench

Every year, someone somewhere decides to rank American cities against each other in wildly specific categories, and every year, the results spark exactly the kind of regional pride and outrage you'd expect. Here's your lighthearted tour through the winners, losers, and everything in between.

## The Singles Scene Champions

Miami, Denver, and Austin consistently duke it out for the title of Best City to Be Single In, and honestly, it makes sense. Miami brings the glamour and nightlife, Denver offers the "let's hike then get tacos" energy that apparently works wonders for chemistry, and Austin has enough live music venues to fuel a thousand meet-cutes. If you're perpetually single and blaming your zip code, maybe it's time to consider a move.

## Cleanliness Kings

Cities like Irvine, California, and various tidy Midwestern suburbs tend to sweep the cleanliness categories, probably because they were designed by people who really, really like grid systems and homeowners' associations with teeth. Meanwhile, some beloved historic cities—looking at you, cities with charming-but-questionable sidewalks—rank lower, proving that character and cleanliness don't always hold hands.

## Best People-Watching

New York City and New Orleans routinely top this category, which surprises absolutely no one. NYC gives you Wall Street types speed-walking past street performers past someone in an elaborate costume for no discernible reason. New Orleans just says "hold my beer" and delivers Mardi Gras energy 365 days a year. Sitting on a bench in either city is basically dinner theater, minus the dinner.

## Now For the Rankings Nobody Wants

Every list needs its cellar-dwellers, and the "least attractive" and "least friendly" categories tend to go to cities that, frankly, didn't sign up for this. Certain rust belt cities and overly business-focused metros often land at the bottom of friendliness surveys, with residents supposedly too busy or too guarded for small talk. And attractiveness rankings—let's be honest—are wildly subjective and probably just reflect whoever answered the survey that day.

The truth is, these lists are more fun than scientific. Your hometown might rank last in friendliness one year and crack the top ten the next, depending entirely on who got surveyed and what mood they were in. So take it all with a grain of salt, a sense of humor, and maybe a road trip itinerary to see for yourself.
